opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a very reasonable decision, and I don't read it as a verdict that linear attention or hybrid architectures have failed. MiniMax was one of the first teams to really push a hybrid linear attention model at scale with M1, using lightning attention mixed with softmax layers, so when they went back to full attention for M2, a lot of people interpreted it as "linear attention doesn't work." I'd say the picture is more nuanced than that.

First, there's the question of what you're optimizing for. M2 was positioned very heavily around agentic use cases and coding, things like multi-step tool use and complex reasoning over long trajectories. In those settings, the bottleneck for the product isn't purely efficiency; it's reliability. And the honest situation is that for some capabilities, especially precise retrieval over long context and certain kinds of multi-hop reasoning, hybrid models still have gaps that aren't always visible on standard benchmarks. Their own write-up said roughly this: on the usual leaderboards things looked fine, but when they evaluated more complex, realistic tasks, they saw deficiencies. If you're a company shipping a flagship model, you don't want to take that risk.

Second, there's an infrastructure argument that people underestimate. Full attention has years of ecosystem work behind it: FlashAttention, paged KV cache, prefix caching, speculative decoding, all the serving frameworks. Linear attention and hybrids are much less mature on the inference side. Things like prefix caching become trickier when your state is a recurrent state rather than a KV cache, and low-precision numerics can be more fragile for recurrent states. So the theoretical efficiency advantage doesn't automatically become a real-world cost advantage, especially at the context lengths most users actually use today.

Third, evaluation itself is a problem. We don't yet have good, cheap proxies that tell you during pretraining whether a hybrid will hold up on difficult agentic tasks after RL. When you can't measure the risk, the conservative choice is full attention.

So my interpretation is: it's a pragmatic engineering decision under current constraints, not a fundamental statement. As context lengths grow, with agents running for hours and accumulating huge trajectories, the cost of quadratic attention and a growing KV cache becomes much harder to ignore. I think we'll see more efficient architectures come back, probably in better-designed hybrid forms with stronger linear layers like gated delta-rule variants, smarter placement of full attention layers, and more mature kernels and serving support. In fact, other labs, such as Qwen with Qwen3-Next and Kimi with their linear attention work, have kept pushing in that direction. MiniMax's move tells us that the research community has more homework to do, especially on evaluation and infrastructure, rather than that the direction is wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says standard benchmarks missed deficiencies on complex tasks, including multi-hop reasoning, but does not connect those evaluation limits to MiniMax’s initial choice of linear attention.

r002.rationale: It anticipates future hybrid designs with stronger linear layers, but does not say MiniMax’s chosen method was outdated relative to later advances.

r003.rationale: It identifies multi-hop reasoning gaps as a concern behind M2’s focus on reliability, but does not clearly state a substantial performance gap between MiniMax’s linear attention and full attention.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a very pragmatic decision, and honestly, I don't read it as a verdict against linear attention or hybrid architectures in general. It's more a statement about where the engineering ecosystem is right now.

If you look back at M1, they did lightning attention, a hybrid with roughly a seven-to-one ratio of linear layers to full attention layers. The research motivation was clear: at long context, softmax attention is quadratic in compute and the KV cache grows linearly, so a mostly-linear hybrid should give you a big efficiency win. And on paper it does. But when they actually tried to productionize it and push the model toward agentic, multi-step reasoning workloads, they ran into a few problems that I think are quite representative.

The first is infrastructure. Full attention has had years of optimization: FlashAttention, paged KV cache, speculative decoding, prefix caching, all the serving tricks in vLLM and SGLang. Everything is built around the assumption that your model is a standard Transformer. The moment you have a recurrent state instead of a KV cache, a lot of that stops working out of the box. Prefix caching with a linear state is a different problem. Speculative decoding with a recurrent state needs to handle rollback. Low-precision inference is trickier because the state accumulates error. None of this is impossible, we've been working on exactly these things in the flash-linear-attention community, but for a company that needs to ship a competitive model this quarter, each of these is a real cost. So the theoretical efficiency gain gets eaten by implementation overhead.

The second issue, and I think this is the more interesting one scientifically, is evaluation. Hybrid models often look fine on standard benchmarks, perplexity, MMLU-style things, even needle-in-a-haystack. Where they tend to show weakness is on tasks that require precise retrieval and manipulation of many tokens over a long horizon. Multi-turn agentic coding, tool use with long trajectories, complex in-context learning. The linear state has a fixed capacity, so it's inherently lossy, and the one-in-eight full attention layers have to do a lot of heavy lifting to compensate. My understanding is that MiniMax found these gaps only showed up at scale and on the exact workloads they cared about, which is the worst possible time to discover them. If your evaluation suite doesn't surface these differences early, you can't do architecture iteration cheaply.

So from their position, going back to full attention in M2 is the lower-risk path. You can focus all your energy on data, RL, and the agentic capability itself, instead of fighting the architecture.

That said, I don't think this is the end of the story at all. A few points. One, the fact that the first-wave hybrid models hit these issues tells us what the research community needs to fix: better state-capacity mechanisms, things like delta-rule-based updates or gated variants that can actually overwrite and retrieve more precisely rather than just decaying. Two, the infrastructure gap is closable, and it's closing. Three, the economics haven't changed. If agents are going to run with hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens of context, full attention's KV cache cost becomes a real bottleneck, and the pressure to find something better will come back. We've already seen other labs, Qwen with Gated DeltaNet in Qwen3-Next, Kimi with their linear attention work, continue to go in the hybrid direction even as MiniMax stepped back.

So I'd summarize it as: MiniMax made the right call for their business timeline, and it's a useful data point for the field about what actually matters when you deploy these architectures. But it's a tactical retreat, not a refutation. The question of how to get sub-quadratic attention to match full attention on hard retrieval and reasoning tasks is still very open, and it's exactly the kind of thing that keeps me motivated to work on it.

astra-6.text:
My interpretation is that MiniMax is making a pragmatic trade-off. Full attention is expensive, but it gives each token direct access to the preceding context. Architectures that compress that context can be more efficient, but the question is what information gets lost—and whether that loss matters for the tasks you care about.

If M2 is returning to full attention, I’d read that as a signal that, for this model, the capability benefits outweighed the efficiency gains of the alternative. That could matter especially when a task requires retrieving a small detail from a long context or maintaining precise dependencies across many steps. But we shouldn’t infer their exact motivation from the architecture choice alone.

I also wouldn’t call it a verdict against linear attention. An architecture has to work as part of a whole system: training stability, hardware utilization, inference cost, and model quality all matter. A theoretically cheaper attention mechanism doesn’t automatically produce the best practical model. To me, the interesting question is what trade-off changed enough to make full attention the better choice for M2.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d interpret it as a pragmatic engineering choice. If full attention gave them the best balance of model quality, training stability, and inference efficiency for M2, then returning to it makes sense. An architecture has to earn its place through results.

Linear attention has an attractive scaling advantage, especially for long contexts, but that doesn’t automatically translate into a better model at a given compute budget. You also have to consider how well it preserves information and how efficiently it runs on the hardware you actually use.

Without their internal ablations, I wouldn’t claim to know which factor drove the decision. My takeaway is narrower: for M2, they judged full attention to be the better tradeoff. That’s useful evidence, but it doesn’t settle the broader question of which architecture will win over time.
